claim: HIV-1 presents an important global health issue with >36 million people infected worldwide and 2.1 million newly acquired infections in 2015.
source: HIV-1 presents an important global health issue with >36 million people infected worldwide and 2.1 million newly acquired infections in 2015.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to UNAIDS, 2015 data.

claim: The majority of new HIV-1 infections result from heterosexual transmission, with women accounting for a majority of all new infections worldwide.
source: The majority of new HIV-1 infections result from heterosexual transmission, with women accounting for a majority of all new infections worldwide (UNAIDS, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to UNAIDS, 2015.

claim: Blood contains only 1–2% of HIV-1 target cells in the body.
source: With blood containing only 1–2% of HIV-1 target cells in the body, the majority of HIV-1 target cells in the human body reside within tissues (Guy-Grand and Vassalli, 1993; Kilby, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guy-Grand and Vassalli, 1993 and Kilby, 2001.

claim: The majority of HIV-1 target cells in the human body reside within tissues.
source: With blood containing only 1–2% of HIV-1 target cells in the body, the majority of HIV-1 target cells in the human body reside within tissues (Guy-Grand and Vassalli, 1993; Kilby, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guy-Grand and Vassalli, 1993 and Kilby, 2001.

claim: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), lymph nodes, and spleen contain a large number HIV-1 target cells that support localized virus transmission and remain a key source of virus replication during systemic spread and long term disease progression.
source: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), lymph nodes, and spleen contain a large number HIV-1 target cells that support localized virus transmission and remain a key source of virus replication during systemic spread and long term disease progression (Haase, 1999; Reinhart et al., 1997; Grossman et al., 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haase, 1999; Reinhart et al., 1997; Grossman et al., 1998.

claim: Mice with humanized immune systems (hu-mice) allow the rapid generation of human target cells infected with wildtype virus in a living organism with a functioning immune system.
source: Mice with humanized immune systems (hu-mice) allow the rapid generation of human target cells infected with wildtype virus in a living organism with a functioning immune system and recapitulate important aspects of HIV-1 pathology including mucosal infection, systemic virus spread, latency, and response to therapeutic intervention (Hatziioannou and Evans, 2012; Marsden and Zack, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hatziioannou and Evans, 2012; Marsden and Zack, 2015.

claim: Hu-mice recapitulate important aspects of HIV-1 pathology including mucosal infection, systemic virus spread, latency, and response to therapeutic intervention.
source: Mice with humanized immune systems (hu-mice) allow the rapid generation of human target cells infected with wildtype virus in a living organism with a functioning immune system and recapitulate important aspects of HIV-1 pathology including mucosal infection, systemic virus spread, latency, and response to therapeutic intervention (Hatziioannou and Evans, 2012; Marsden and Zack, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hatziioannou and Evans, 2012; Marsden and Zack, 2015.

claim: PBMC-NSG mice rapidly reconstitute human CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells in addition to human B-cells.
source: PBMC-NSG mice rapidly reconstitute human CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells in addition to human B-cells and disseminate human lymphoid cells to lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow, genital mucosa, and intestine (Hatziioannou and Evans, 2012; Marsden and Zack, 2015; Ishikawa et al., 2005; King et al., 2008; Mosier et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hatziioannou and Evans, 2012; Marsden and Zack, 2015; Ishikawa et al., 2005; King et al., 2008; Mosier et al., 1988.

claim: PBMC-NSG mice disseminate human lymphoid cells to lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow, genital mucosa, and intestine.
source: PBMC-NSG mice rapidly reconstitute human CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells in addition to human B-cells and disseminate human lymphoid cells to lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow, genital mucosa, and intestine (Hatziioannou and Evans, 2012; Marsden and Zack, 2015; Ishikawa et al., 2005; King et al., 2008; Mosier et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hatziioannou and Evans, 2012; Marsden and Zack, 2015; Ishikawa et al., 2005; King et al., 2008; Mosier et al., 1988.

claim: CD4+ T-cells make up the majority of all HIV-1 target cells in humans.
source: CD4+ T-cells make up the majority of all HIV-1 target cells in humans (Haase, 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haase, 1999.

claim: Activated T cells constitute approximately 10% of all CD4+ T cells in humans.
source: activated T cells constitute a sizeable proportion of all CD4+ T cells in humans (~10%)
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Activated T cells rise to approximately 20–40% during the course of HIV-1 infection.
source: activated T cells rise to ~20–40% during the course of HIV-1 infection (Mahalingam et al., 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mahalingam et al., 1993.

claim: Activated T cells localize to important tissue sites of virus pathology including spleen, lymph nodes, and GALT.
source: activated T cells localize to important tissue sites of virus pathology including spleen, lymph nodes, and GALT (Saksena et al., 2010; Cerf-Bensussan and Guy-Grand, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Saksena et al., 2010; Cerf-Bensussan and Guy-Grand, 1991.

claim: HIV-1 infection of PBMC-NSG mice mimics early stages of infection in humans, in that the virus replicates exponentially, resulting in large scale CD4+ T-cell depletion within a few weeks.
source: HIV-1 infection of PBMC-NSG mice mimics early stages of infection in humans, in that the virus replicates exponentially, resulting in large scale CD4+ T-cell depletion within a few weeks (Marsden and Zack, 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marsden and Zack, 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2008.

claim: HIV-1-infected PBMC-NSG mice normally show robust blood p24 levels approximately 2–4 weeks post-infection, followed by a sharp decrease of viral load.
source: HIV-1-infected PBMC-NSG mice normally show robust blood p24 levels ~2–4 weeks post-infection (PI), followed by a sharp decrease of viral load (Kim et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2008; Balazs et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2008; Balazs et al., 2012, 2014.

claim: Blood p24 levels in HIV-1 infected BLT mice regularly peak at approximately 4–6 weeks PI, followed by a slower reduction in blood viral load.
source: blood p24 levels in HIV-1 infected BLT mice regularly peak at ~4–6 weeks PI, followed by a slower reduction in blood viral load (Sun et al., 2007; Brainard et al., 2009; Denton et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sun et al., 2007; Brainard et al., 2009; Denton et al., 2008.

claim: HIV-1 p24 levels in blood showed mean levels of 2.50 ± 0.78 ng/mL at 12 days PI and 12.68 ± 8.05 ng/mL at 21 days PI in three infected PBMC-NSG mice.
source: HIV-1 p24 levels in blood showed mean levels of 2.50 ± 0.78 ng/mL at 12 days PI and 12.68 ± 8.05 ng/mL at 21 days PI, demonstrating productive infection in all three animals (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IF of colon showed the presence of human CD3+ cells and HIV-1 p24 in infected animals three weeks PI in colon crypts and within the crypt epithelium.
source: IF of colon showed the presence of human CD3+ cells and HIV-1 p24 in infected animals three weeks PI in colon crypts and within the crypt epithelium (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ET corroborated the IF results, showing the presence of infected cells indicated by virus budding profiles projecting from the plasma membrane and free virions in similar tissue locations.
source: ET corroborated the IF results, showing the presence of infected cells indicated by virus budding profiles projecting from the plasma membrane and free virions in similar tissue locations (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: The localization and levels of T-cells and HIV-1 within colon crypts were consistent with previous studies in HIV-1–infected BLT animals.
source: The localization and levels of T-cells and HIV-1 within colon crypts were consistent with our previous studies in HIV-1–infected BLT animals (Ladinsky et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ladinsky et al., 2014.

claim: Optical clearing techniques offer the opportunity to image large volumes of opaque tissues by IF without serial sectioning.
source: Optical clearing techniques offer the opportunity to image large volumes of opaque tissues by IF without serial sectioning (Richardson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Richardson et al., 2015.

claim: GALT and female reproductive tract (FRT) were cleared using CLARITY/PACT.
source: GALT and female reproductive tract (FRT) were cleared using CLARITY/PACT (Treweek et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method used and is supported by citation to Treweek et al., 2015.

claim: Spleen samples containing heme were cleared using CUBIC.
source: spleen samples containing heme were cleared using CUBIC (Tainaka et al., 2014) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method used and is supported by citation to Tainaka et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: IF of cleared GALT from uninfected animals revealed human CD3+ T-cells in the colon, spleen, and FRT.
source: IF of cleared GALT from uninfected animals revealed human CD3+ T-cells in the colon, spleen, and FRT (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Confocal microscopy in different lymphoid tissues from HIV-1–infected PBMC-NSG mice revealed the presence of human CD3+ T-cells, a subset of which were positive for HIV-1 p24.
source: Confocal microscopy in different lymphoid tissues from HIV-1–infected PBMC-NSG mice revealed the presence of human CD3+ T-cells, a subset of which were positive for HIV-1 p24 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Some regions of p24 staining were not positive for human CD3, representing either free HIV-1 virions or infected cells other than T cells.
source: Some regions of p24 staining were not positive for human CD3, representing either free HIV-1 virions or infected cells other than T cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Representative images revealed low levels of infected human CD3+ T-cells at 5 days PI, which rapidly increased to peak levels at 10–16 days PI, before diminishing at time points >21 days PI.
source: Representative images revealed low levels of infected human CD3+ T-cells at 5 days PI, which rapidly increased to peak levels at 10–16 days PI, before diminishing at time points >21 days PI.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from representative images in the manuscript.

claim: Automated quantification of nuclei resulted in an agreement of 96.2 ± 1.9% compared to manual quantification.
source: the total number of nuclei in confocal slices were determined using the Fiji software suite (Schindelin et al., 2012), resulting in an agreement of 96.2 ± 1.9% compared to manual quantification (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: T-cells in colon from uninfected PBMC-NSG mice remained near 6% of total cells.
source: T-cells in colon from uninfected PBMC-NSG mice remained near 6% of total cells (Figure 3C)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: T-cell density in colon from uninfected PBMC-NSG mice is comparable to the approximately 10–12% found in uninfected human patient samples.
source: T-cells in colon from uninfected PBMC-NSG mice remained near 6% of total cells (Figure 3C), comparable to the ~10–12% found in uninfected human patient samples (McElrath et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McElrath et al., 2013.

claim: Human CD3+ T-cell densities in HIV-1–infected animals were similar to densities in uninfected controls until 12 days PI, at which time T-cell levels rapidly dropped to <4% of total cells at 16 days PI and continued to decrease gradually out to 45 days PI.
source: Human CD3+ T-cell densities in HIV-1–infected animals were similar to densities in uninfected controls until 12 days PI, at which time T-cell levels rapidly dropped to <4% of total cells at 16 days PI and continued to decrease gradually out to 45 days PI.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data from the study.

claim: Peak infectivity in GALT occurred at 12 days PI, with nearly 3% of cells representing HIV-1–infected T-cells.
source: p24+/human CD3+ T-cells were quantified similarly in GALT, revealing peak infectivity at 12 days PI, with nearly 3% of cells representing HIV-1–infected T-cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GALT infectivity levels rapidly decreased to <1% of cells representing infected T-cells after 21 days PI and approached zero by 35 days PI.
source: Infectivity levels rapidly decreased to <1% of cells representing infected T-cells after 21 days PI and approached zero by 35 days PI.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data from the study.

claim: The percent of p24+ T-cells peaked at 12 days PI and preceded peak blood p24 levels by 9 days, when p24 levels were low.
source: When compared to p24 levels in blood from the same animals, the percent of p24+ T-cells peaked at 12 days PI and preceded peak blood p24 levels by 9 days, when p24 levels were low (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At peak blood p24 levels (21 days PI), the percentage of p24+ T-cells in colon had already diminished to nearly half of maximum levels at 10–12 days PI.
source: At peak blood p24 levels (21 days PI), the percentage of p24+ T-cells in colon had already diminished to nearly half of maximum levels at 10–12 days PI.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data from the study.

claim: There is a disconnect between tissue infectivity and blood viral load over time.
source: These results are consistent with a disconnect between tissue infectivity and blood viral load over time, as previously noted in human samples (Anton et al., 2003; Chun et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anton et al., 2003; Chun et al., 1997.

claim: There was an increase in p24 signal not associated with human CD3+ T-cells concomitant with decreased infectivity of human CD3+ T-cells at 21 days PI.
source: This analysis revealed an increase in p24 signal not associated with human CD3+ T-cells concomitant with decreased infectivity of human CD3+ T-cells at 21 days PI.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data from the study.

claim: A 45 μm confocal Z-stack from the colon of an HIV-1–infected hu-mouse at 12 days PI displayed human CD4+ T-cells and p24+ cells localized to intestinal crypts and the bottom half of villi.
source: A 45 μm confocal Z-stack from the colon of an HIV-1–infected hu-mouse at 12 days PI displayed human CD4+ T-cells and p24+ cells localized to intestinal crypts and the bottom half of villi, whereas human CD8+ T-cells were dispersed uniformly throughout the crypts and the length of the villi (Figure 4A,B and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A,B and Video 1.

claim: Human CD8+ T-cells were dispersed uniformly throughout the crypts and the length of the villi.
source: A 45 μm confocal Z-stack from the colon of an HIV-1–infected hu-mouse at 12 days PI displayed human CD4+ T-cells and p24+ cells localized to intestinal crypts and the bottom half of villi, whereas human CD8+ T-cells were dispersed uniformly throughout the crypts and the length of the villi (Figure 4A,B and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A,B and Video 1.

claim: Mean distances from the base of crypts were 51.2 ± 34.5 μm for human CD4+ T-cells, 79.2 ± 36.8 μm for human CD8+ T-cells, and 47.9 ± 45.1 μm for p24+ cells.
source: Mean distances from the base of crypts were 51.2 ± 34.5 μm for human CD4+ T-cells, 79.2 ± 36.8 μm for human CD8+ T-cells, and 47.9 ± 45.1 μm for p24+ cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The localization of HIV-1–infected cells to colon crypts is consistent with previous EM and IF studies of later stages of HIV-1 infection in GALT from BLT hu-mice.
source: The localization of HIV-1–infected cells to colon crypts is consistent with our previous EM and IF studies of later stages of HIV-1 infection in GALT from BLT hu-mice (Ladinsky et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ladinsky et al., 2014.

claim: The localization of HIV-1–infected cells to colon crypts is consistent with results from early SIV infection in rhesus macaques.
source: The localization of HIV-1–infected cells to colon crypts is consistent with our previous EM and IF studies of later stages of HIV-1 infection in GALT from BLT hu-mice (Ladinsky et al., 2014) and with results from early SIV infection in rhesus macaques (Hirao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hirao et al., 2014.

claim: The spatial arrangement of cell types (CD4+, CD8+, and p24+) remained constant during the course of the experiment.
source: The spatial arrangement of these cell types remained constant during the course of the experiment (Figure 4D)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The total numbers of human CD4+ T-cells and p24+ cells markedly decreased at late time points.
source: even as the total numbers of human CD4+ T-cells and p24+ cells markedly decreased at late time points (Figure 4E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The decrease in CD4+ T-cells and p24+ cells at late time points is likely due to target cell depletion.
source: even as the total numbers of human CD4+ T-cells and p24+ cells markedly decreased at late time points (Figure 4E), likely due to target cell depletion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed data.

claim: Early after infection (5 days PI), infected cells and free virus were not readily detected by EM.
source: Early after infection (5 days PI), infected cells and free virus were not readily detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data from the study.

claim: There was an exponential increase in the number of infected cells and the presence of large extracellular pools of free virus during peak infectivity (10–16 days PI).
source: This was followed by an exponential increase in the number of infected cells and the presence of large extracellular pools of free virus, often containing >100 free virions within 200–400 nm thick regions of tissue during peak infectivity (10–16 days PI).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data from the study.

claim: At peak infectivity (10–16 days PI), approximately 10% of crypts showed signs of active infection cells as evidenced by cells with budding virions attached to the plasma membrane.
source: At this time, ~10% of crypts showed signs of active infection cells as evidenced by cells with budding virions attached to the plasma membrane (Figure 5B; center panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At later times (>21 days PI), the total number of infected cells was reduced and individual pools of free virus in similar locations contained fewer virions.
source: At later times (>21 days PI), the total number of infected cells was reduced and individual pools of free virus in similar locations contained fewer virions.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data from the study.

claim: Most of the pools of free virus at later times (>21 days PI) were not associated with actively-infected cells.
source: Most of the pools of free virus were not associated with actively-infected cells, consistent with our IF observation that levels of HIV-1 p24 not associated with human CD3+ T-cells increased at later time points PI (Figure 3B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data and is consistent with IF observations.

claim: Most of the p24+/CD3- cells detected by IF at late times PI represented pools of free-virions, rather than infected cells other than T cells.
source: These results suggested that most of the p24+/CD3- cells detected by IF at late times PI represented pools of free-virions, rather than infected cells other than T cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EM and IF data.

claim: Pools of virus in lamina propria were often found near vasculature.
source: Pools of virus in lamina propria were often found near vasculature, and ET allowed tracing of a virus-containing lateral intercellular space in 3D exhibiting pools of virus with openings leading to the walls of blood vessels (Figure 5C; right panels and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data shown in Figure 5C and Video 2.

claim: ET allowed tracing of a virus-containing lateral intercellular space in 3D exhibiting pools of virus with openings leading to the walls of blood vessels.
source: Pools of virus in lamina propria were often found near vasculature, and ET allowed tracing of a virus-containing lateral intercellular space in 3D exhibiting pools of virus with openings leading to the walls of blood vessels (Figure 5C; right panels and Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data shown in Figure 5C and Video 2.

claim: Splenic tissue can be histologically divided into regions of red and white pulp.
source: Splenic tissue can be histologically divided into regions of red and white pulp (Mebius and Kraal, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mebius and Kraal, 2005.

claim: Red pulp makes up a majority of the volume of the spleen, contains large numbers of red blood cells generating a red hue, and primarily functions to filter the blood.
source: Red pulp makes up a majority of the volume of the spleen, contains large numbers of red blood cells (RBCs) generating a red hue, and primarily functions to filter the blood.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about spleen anatomy.

claim: White pulp contains large numbers of B- and T-cells that coordinate immune responses within the blood.
source: White pulp contains large numbers of B- and T-cells that coordinate immune responses within the blood.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about spleen anatomy.

claim: Spleen harbors large quantities of HIV-1 target cells, making it an important organ for HIV-1 pathology.
source: As such, spleen harbors large quantities of HIV-1 target cells, making it an important organ for HIV-1 pathology (Mebius and Kraal, 2005; Ganusov and De Boer, 2007; Langeveld et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mebius and Kraal, 2005; Ganusov and De Boer, 2007; Langeveld et al., 2006.

claim: A longitudinal study of SIV infection in NHP spleen revealed large numbers of HIV-1–infected CD4+ T-cells during acute infection that resulted in T-cell depletion and morphological changes in tissue at later stages of infection.
source: Indeed, a longitudinal study of SIV infection in NHP spleen revealed large numbers of HIV-1–infected CD4+ T-cells during acute infection that resulted in T-cell depletion and morphological changes in tissue at later stages of infection (Williams et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Williams et al., 2016.

claim: The findings from SIV infection in NHP spleen are consistent with human autopsy studies.
source: a longitudinal study of SIV infection in NHP spleen revealed large numbers of HIV-1–infected CD4+ T-cells during acute infection that resulted in T-cell depletion and morphological changes in tissue at later stages of infection (Williams et al., 2016), consistent with human autopsy studies (Diaz et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Diaz et al., 2002.

claim: Brightfield microscopy of spleen from non-reconstituted NSG animals showed little to no white pulp.
source: EM of white pulp from wildtype animals revealed diverse cell types, including lymphocytes, and collagen deposits. In contrast, brightfied microscopy of spleen from non-reconstituted NSG animals showed little to no white pulp
evidence: This claim is supported by brightfield microscopy data from the study.

claim: EM of NSG spleen samples indicated different cell types, denser packing, and little collagen compared to wildtype spleen.
source: EM of these samples indicated different cell types, denser packing, and little collagen (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: IF of uninfected PBMC-NSG spleen showed localized pockets of human CD3+ T-cells interspersed throughout volumes of splenic tissue.
source: IF of uninfected PBMC-NSG spleen showed localized pockets of human CD3+ T-cells interspersed throughout volumes of splenic tissue (Figures 2B and 6A; left panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by IF data shown in Figures 2B and 6A.

claim: Montaged projection EM surveys of uninfected PBMC-NSG spleen demonstrated delineations between white pulp and red pulp regions.
source: Montaged projection EM surveys of uninfected PBMC-NSG spleen demonstrated delineations between white pulp and red pulp regions (Figure 6B; left panels and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Red pulp in PBMC-NSG spleen contained enucleated RBCs.
source: Red pulp contained enucleated RBCs
evidence: This claim is supported by EM observations from the study.

claim: White pulp in PBMC-NSG spleen was distinguished by an absence of RBCs, bundles of collagen fibrils, and populations of lymphocytes identified as cells with large, dense nuclei surrounded by minimal cytoplasm.
source: while white pulp was distinguished by an absence of RBCs, bundles of collagen fibrils, and populations of lymphocytes identified as cells with large, dense nuclei surrounded by minimal cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM observations from the study.

claim: The organization of the spleen in PBMC-NSG hu-mice was intermediary between non-reconstituted NSG animals and wildtype immunocompetent animals.
source: Overall, the organization of the spleen in PBMC-NSG hu-mice was intermediary between non-reconstituted NSG animals and wildtype immunocompetent animals, with white pulp occurring as smaller striations within the red pulp as opposed to the circular foci seen in spleens from wildtype animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Structural and cellular components of splenic white pulp, most importantly HIV-1 target cells, are present in PBMC-NSG animals even though the splenic architecture is altered.
source: These results demonstrated that structural and cellular components of splenic white pulp, most importantly HIV-1 target cells, are present in PBMC-NSG animals even though the splenic architecture is altered.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EM and IF data.

claim: IF of spleen from an HIV-1–infected PBMC-NSG animal at 12 days PI revealed the presence of human CD3+ T-cells in addition to sporadic foci of HIV-1 p24 distributed throughout large regions of tissue.
source: IF of spleen revealed the presence of human CD3+ T-cells in addition to sporadic foci of HIV-1 p24 distributed throughout large regions of tissue (Figure 6A, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by IF data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: EM of spleen from an HIV-1–infected animal at 12 days PI showed discernable regions of white pulp containing infected lymphocytes intercalated within bundles of collagen fibrils and surrounded by HIV-1 virions.
source: EM of spleen from the same animal showed discernable regions of white pulp containing infected lymphocytes intercalated within bundles of collagen fibrils and surrounded by HIV-1 virions (Figure 6B; right panel and Figure 7A,B; top panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 7A,B.

claim: ET of an HIV-1–infected cell from spleen 12 days PI revealed prolific virus production at distinct regions of plasma membrane.
source: ET of an HIV-1–infected cell from spleen 12 days PI revealed prolific virus production at distinct regions of plasma membrane (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Serial section tomographic reconstruction of a 6.9 μm x 3.5 μm x 0.8 μm (19.3 μm3) volume from a single infected cell contained nearly 1000 virus particles of which 846 were mature, 18 were immature, and 102 were budding from the cell surface.
source: Serial section tomographic reconstruction of a 6.9 μm x 3.5 μm x 0.8 μm (19.3 μm3) volume from a single infected cell contained nearly 1000 virus particles of which 846 were mature, 18 were immature, and 102 were budding from the cell surface (Figure 7A and Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data shown in Figure 7A and Video 3.

claim: A single cell could produce >6000 virions during a single round of virus production.
source: By approximating the volume of an entire cell as an ellipsoid, we used this result to calculate that a single cell could produce >6000 virions during a single round of virus production.
evidence: This claim is based on calculation from the ET data.

claim: A reconstructed 3.4 μm x 3.4 μm x 1.2 μm (13.9 μm3) volume from another HIV-1–infected cell in spleen at 12 days PI revealed 1350 virus particles with 1329 mature, 15 immature, six budding virions, and predicted >4000 virions released.
source: A reconstructed 3.4 μm x 3.4 μm x 1.2 μm (13.9 μm3) volume from another HIV-1–infected cell in spleen at the same time PI revealed 1350 virus particles with 1329 mature, 15 immature, six budding virions, and predicted >4000 virions released (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: VPS4 is a hexameric AAA+ ATPase recruited by the endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT) protein network to enable the fission of membranes during cellular processes including cell division, endosomal sorting, and virus budding.
source: VPS4 is a hexameric AAA+ ATPase (Monroe et al., 2014) recruited by the endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT) protein network to enable the fission of membranes during cellular processes including cell division, endosomal sorting, and virus budding (Sundquist and Kräusslich, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Monroe et al., 2014 and Sundquist and Kräusslich, 2012.

claim: In previous ET studies of HIV-1 infection in GALT from BLT hu-mice, discreet densities localized at the base of budding virions were identified and proposed to include VPS4 oligomers.
source: In previous ET studies of HIV-1 infection in GALT from BLT hu-mice, we identified discreet densities localized at the base of budding virions and proposed that they included VPS4 oligomers (Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ladinsky et al., 2014.

claim: Similar densities to those previously identified were found localizing to the base of budding virions in tomograms of splenic tissue from HIV-1-infected PBMC-NSG mice at 12 days PI.
source: We found similar densities localizing to the base of budding virions in tomograms of splenic tissue from HIV-1-infected PBMC-NSG mice at 12 days PI (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Immuno-EM using an anti-VPS4 antibody showed localization of VPS4 to the base of budding virions.
source: Immuno-EM using an anti-VPS4 antibody showed localization of VPS4 to the base of budding virions (Figure 8B)
evidence: This claim is supported by immuno-EM data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The localization of VPS4 to the base of budding virions suggests that the densities include VPS4, perhaps in complex with other proteins.
source: demonstrating that VPS4 localizes to the same region, suggesting that the densities include VPS4, perhaps in complex with other proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the immuno-EM data.

claim: In some cells, ET revealed large numbers of virions (>100 budding profiles) produced from distinct regions of the plasma membrane of HIV-1–infected cells.
source: In some cells, ET revealed large numbers of virions (>100 budding profiles) produced from distinct regions of the plasma membrane of HIV-1–infected cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: In the cytoplasm immediately adjacent to sites of prolific virus release, accumulations of large numbers of densities indistinguishable from the densities near budding virions were found.
source: In the cytoplasm immediately adjacent to these sites of prolific virus release, we found accumulations of large numbers of densities indistinguishable from the densities near budding virions (Figures 8C,D and 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data shown in Figures 8C,D and 9.

claim: Cytoplasmic densities were found in direct proximity (within 1 µm of the plasma membrane) to large numbers of budding virions and contained hundreds to thousands of densities within an individual accumulation.
source: These cytoplasmic densities were found in direct proximity (within 1 µm of the plasma membrane) to large numbers of budding virions and contained hundreds to thousands of densities within an individual accumulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ET observations from the study.

claim: The cytoplasmic densities are not ribosomes, since they were more electron dense than neighboring ribosomes and also lacked the characteristic cleft between the small and large ribosomal subunits.
source: However, we ruled out identification of the densities as ribosomes, since they were more electron dense than neighboring ribosomes and also lacked the characteristic cleft between the small and large ribosomal subunits (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of ET data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The cytoplasmic densities were not found in infected lymphocytes in the splenic white pulp that were surrounded by large pools of free virions but displayed few budding profiles (<10 buds).
source: The cytoplasmic densities were not found in infected lymphocytes in the splenic white pulp that were surrounded by large pools of free virions but displayed few budding profiles (<10 buds)
evidence: This claim is supported by ET observations from the study.

claim: Large cytoplasmic pools of density were absent in a cell that exhibited only six budding profiles but was surrounded by >1000 free extracellular virions.
source: large cytoplasmic pools of density were absent in a cell that exhibited only six budding profiles (some of which also included the densities at the bases of the buds) but was surrounded by >1000 free extracellular virions (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Accumulations of cytoplasmic densities were only seen in cells undergoing prolific virus budding, and in these cells, only in regions adjacent to the buds.
source: Indeed, accumulations of cytoplasmic densities were only seen in cells undergoing prolific virus budding, and in these cells, only in regions adjacent to the buds (Figure 8D and Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data shown in Figure 8D and Video 4.

claim: Cytoplasmic pools of densities accumulate during periods of prolific virus production and are exhausted following a round of virus release.
source: These results suggest that cytoplasmic pools of these densities accumulate during periods of prolific virus production and are exhausted following a round of virus release.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the ET observations.

claim: Immunofluorescence revealed peak infection density in gut at 10–12 days post-infection when blood viral loads were low.
source: Immunofluorescence revealed peak infection density in gut at 10–12 days post-infection when blood viral loads were low.
evidence: This claim is supported by IF and blood viral load data from the study.

claim: Human CD4+ T-cells and HIV-1–infected cells localized predominantly to crypts and the lower third of intestinal villi.
source: Human CD4+ T-cells and HIV-1–infected cells localized predominantly to crypts and the lower third of intestinal villi.
evidence: This claim is supported by IF and ET data from the study.

claim: Free virions and infected cells were not readily detectable by ET at 5-days post-infection.
source: Free virions and infected cells were not readily detectable by ET at 5-days post-infection
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data from the study.

claim: HIV-1–infected cells surrounded by pools of free virions were present in approximately 10% of intestinal crypts by 10–12 days post-infection.
source: whereas HIV-1–infected cells surrounded by pools of free virions were present in ~10% of intestinal crypts by 10–12 days.
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data from the study.

claim: ET of spleen revealed thousands of virions released by individual cells.
source: ET of spleen revealed thousands of virions released by individual cells
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data from the study.

claim: ET of spleen revealed discreet cytoplasmic densities near sites of prolific virus production.
source: ET of spleen revealed thousands of virions released by individual cells and discreet cytoplasmic densities near sites of prolific virus production.
evidence: This claim is supported by ET data from the study.

claim: The methods used in this study are adaptable to other animal models and human patient samples.
source: These studies highlight the importance of multiscale imaging of HIV-1–infected tissues and are adaptable to other animal models and human patient samples.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the applicability of the methods.

claim: During heterosexual transmission of HIV-1, the virus crosses the genital epithelium and infects a target cell, which results in localized infection, establishment of a latently-infected virus reservoir, expansion of a local founder population, and systemic virus spread to distant tissues via lymph and blood.
source: During heterosexual transmission of HIV-1, the virus crosses the genital epithelium and infects a target cell, which results in localized infection, establishment of a latently-infected virus reservoir, expansion of a local founder population, and systemic virus spread to distant tissues via lymph and blood (Fackler et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fackler et al., 2014.

claim: The PBMC-NSG hu-mouse model almost exclusively harbors activated human T cells that can react with host antigens and cause animals to develop graft versus host disease.
source: It is important to note that the PBMC-NSG hu-mouse model almost exclusively harbors activated human T cells that can react with host antigens and cause animals to develop graph versus host disease (Marsden and Zack, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marsden and Zack, 2015.

claim: The lack of other cell lineages combined with raised levels of T cell activation in the PBMC-NSG model may enhance the dynamics of HIV spread and pathogenesis compared to other hu-mouse models.
source: The lack of other cell lineages combined with raised levels of T cell activation in this model may enhance the dynamics of HIV spread and pathogenesis compared to other hu-mouse models that contain a smaller compartment of activated T cells at the time of infection and a more diverse set of immune cell lineages.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the model characteristics.

claim: The PBMC-NSG hu-mouse model was previously used to study the effectiveness of anti-HIV-1 therapies in reducing systemic virus spread after intravenous transmission.
source: this model was previously used to study the effectiveness of anti-HIV-1 therapies in reducing systemic virus spread after intravenous transmission (Kim et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2008; Balazs et al., 2012, 2014; Hur et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2008; Balazs et al., 2012, 2014; Hur et al., 2012.

claim: EM was originally utilized to identify HIV-1 as the causative agent of AIDS.
source: EM was originally utilized to identify HIV-1 as the causative agent of AIDS (Barré-Sinoussi et al., 1983; Gallo et al., 1983)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barré-Sinoussi et al., 1983; Gallo et al., 1983.

claim: EM has been applied to examine aspects of HIV-1 pathology at ultrastructural resolution.
source: EM was originally utilized to identify HIV-1 as the causative agent of AIDS (Barré-Sinoussi et al., 1983; Gallo et al., 1983) and has subsequently been applied to examine aspects of HIV-1 pathology at ultrastructural resolution (Orenstein, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Orenstein, 2007.

claim: ET can provide 3D information at subcellular resolution from frozen hydrated or from well-preserved, fixed biological samples.
source: ET can provide 3D information at subcellular resolution from frozen hydrated or from well-preserved, fixed biological samples (McIntosh et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McIntosh et al., 2005.

claim: The total number of SIV virions produced by an individual infected cell was previously estimated to be 4.0–5.4 × 10^4.
source: The total number of SIV virions produced by an individual infected cell was previously estimated to be 4.0–5.4 × 104 (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2007.

claim: If a similar number of HIV-1 virions are produced from infected cells within tissue as SIV virions, this implies multiple rounds of virus release from each infected cell.
source: If a similar number of HIV-1 virions are produced from infected cells within tissue, this implies multiple rounds of virus release from each infected cell, as suggested by our previous ET studies (Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on inference and is supported by citation to Ladinsky et al., 2014.

claim: In lymphoid tissues, the large numbers of target cells combined with high levels of virus production and accessibility to vasculature suggest that HIV-1–infected cells in tissue provide a source of free virus that contributes to blood viral load and systemic spread.
source: In lymphoid tissues, the large numbers of target cells combined with high levels of virus production and accessibility to vasculature suggest that HIV-1–infected cells in tissue provide a source of free virus that contributes to blood viral load and systemic spread.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data.

claim: The parallel multiscale imaging approaches applied in this study allowed visualization of early HIV-1 spread in a hu-mouse model of infection at both single cell and subcellular resolution.
source: In summary, the parallel multiscale imaging approaches applied here allowed visualization of early HIV-1 spread in a hu-mouse model of infection at both single cell and subcellular resolution.
evidence: This claim summarizes the overall findings of the study.

claim: 3D-IF of optically-cleared tissue allowed longitudinal and spatial assessment of the distribution of human T-cells and virus proteins within volumes of intact lymphoid tissue.
source: 3D-IF of optically-cleared tissue allowed us to longitudinally and spatially assess the distribution of human T-cells and virus proteins within volumes of intact lymphoid tissue.
evidence: This claim summarizes the capabilities of the 3D-IF method used in the study.

claim: ET of adjacent regions of tissue allowed the detection of individual virions, infected cells, and subcellular protein complexes within the context of actively-infected tissues at specific times PI.
source: ET of adjacent regions of tissue allowed the detection of individual virions, infected cells, and subcellular protein complexes within the context of actively-infected tissues at specific times PI.
evidence: This claim summarizes the capabilities of the ET method used in the study.

claim: These approaches are directly applicable to additional lymphoid tissues such as lymph nodes, bone marrow, and thymus in infected hu-mouse, NHP, and human patient samples.
source: These approaches are directly applicable to additional lymphoid tissues such as lymph nodes, bone marrow, and thymus in infected hu-mouse, NHP, and human patient samples.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the applicability of the methods.

claim: Future efforts will allow the visualization of discreet biological processes occurring during early HIV-1 spread in lymphoid tissues.
source: Future efforts will allow the visualization of discreet biological processes occurring during early HIV-1 spread in lymphoid tissues and enable the development of a quantifiable spatial map of HIV-1 spread in tissues during early infection.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about future applications.

claim: Future efforts will enable the development of a quantifiable spatial map of HIV-1 spread in tissues during early infection.
source: Future efforts will allow the visualization of discreet biological processes occurring during early HIV-1 spread in lymphoid tissues and enable the development of a quantifiable spatial map of HIV-1 spread in tissues during early infection.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about future applications.
